h: Shabbat's Boundless Inheritance and Yaakov's Exile as the Root of Exiles
Seudah Shelishit and the Boundless Inheritance

p: — Regarding the third meal of Shabbat
— "and I will feed you the inheritance of Yaakov your father"
— like Yaakov, of whom it is written:
— 'and you shall spread out westward,' etc."
— "Avraham, of whom it is not written
— inherited the world in measure, etc.;
— Yaakov, of whom it is written
— that in the merit of Shabbat
— he inherited an inheritance without boundaries.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of the Sabbath 18 (Kabbalah): The Arizal's teaching on the three Shabbat meals calls the third meal "an inheritance without boundaries," because at that hour no kelipah holds sway and Ze'ir Anpin rises close to the "supernal brow" of Atika; this meal is tied to the verse "and I will feed you the inheritance of Yaakov your father." Rav Tzadok builds on the same pairing of the third meal, the boundless inheritance and the revelation of Atika.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Sefat Emet, Genesis, Bereshit 13 (Chassidus): The Torah opens "Bereishit" for the sake of Israel, who are called "reishit," the first-fruit portion of creation that raises the rest of the world to its root; the same piece goes on to the Shabbat delight that earns "a boundless inheritance, the inheritance of Yaakov." It joins reishit, Israel's root in creation, and Shabbat as Rav Tzadok does.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Gevurot Hashem 54 (Machshava): The Maharal asks why the Haggadah passes over Esav and opens with Lavan, of whom Scripture never says he sought to uproot everything. Rav Tzadok gives the same passage a parallel weight, making Lavan the root of all the exiles.

h: Exile as Preparation: Egypt and Babylon

p: — "And the Egyptians did evil to us" —
— "a nation from the midst of a nation,"
— that they were like a fetus
— and they were surrounded and sunk
— for the giving of the Torah,
— the sufferings of the Egyptian exile.
— as it was said to Yaakov:
— I will make of you there" —
— that Yaakov our father did not pass away
— And so too in the Babylonian exile,
— are the children of the desolate one,' etc. —
— did she raise up for Me in her destruction
— she raised up for Me when she was built."
— as a sign for the children.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Shmuel Bornsztain of Sochatchov, Shem MiShmuel, Bo 8:22: “It seems that since Israel in Egypt were like a fetus in an animal’s womb, and a fetus is like its mother’s thigh and eats what its mother eats, the evil traits of Pharaoh and of Egypt worked on them for ill, as the heat of the mother’s blood works on the fetus. This is what is found in the Midrash of the Haggadah: ‘And the Egyptians did evil to us’ is a transitive verb, meaning that they made us evil, and this is the reason. Their insolence and excessive brazenness acted on Israel, seized them with force and drew them toward the trait of brazenness. Nevertheless the community of Israel, who by nature have the good traits that our holy fathers implanted in them, being modest, merciful and doers of kindness, were held by these, so that they stood with all strength against the evil powers of Egypt and were not drawn after them; only Datan and Aviram, who were the refuse of Israel, were drawn.”

h: Accepting the Yoke of Torah in Exile

p: — And so too every soul of Israel
— the day of Shabbat in observance,
— the inheritance of Yaakov your father" —
— that holiness will go with him
— "that I may dwell in the house of Hashem
— all the days of my life," etc.
— "On the day that Hashem gives you rest," etc.,
— with which you were made to serve."
— And it is expounded in the holy Zohar
— as referring to the day of Shabbat,
— which is "the day of giving rest."
— in the midst of the hard labor,
— since on the day of Shabbat
— the yoke of Torah in truth.

paragraphs.text: Pirkei Avot 3:5: "R. Nechunya ben HaKanah says: whoever accepts upon himself the yoke of Torah, they remove from him the yoke of the kingdom and the yoke of worldly affairs." Rav Tzadok stresses "accepts," not "engages": even in exile, when one cannot study, the acceptance itself lifts the yoke of the nations.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefat Emet, Toldot 18:5: “In the Midrash: ‘When the voice is the voice of Yaakov, the hands are not the hands of Esav.’ This is the Mishnah, ‘Whoever accepts upon himself the yoke of Torah, they remove from him the yoke of the kingdom.’ They said ‘remove,’ which implies that even while we are slaves in exile, there is still no person who does not have an hour in which some redemption awakens in his soul, so that he can accept upon himself the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven. Likewise, in general, whoever accepts the yoke of Torah properly certainly helps the redemption, and from him and by his strength the yoke of the kingdom is removed. So too with the yoke of worldly affairs: although one must labor for his livelihood, Hashem gave us the mitzvah of Shabbat, which is a day of rest, as it is taught, ‘Shabbat should be made entirely Torah.’ Every merchant must accept the yoke of Torah on the day of Shabbat, and by its strength the yoke of worldly affairs is removed from him in the days of work.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Sefat Emet, Genesis, Vayetzei 20 (Chassidus): "And Yaakov went out" is both the exile after the Temple and every Motza'ei Shabbat. Yaakov "helps us in exile," so wherever Israel struggle to find a point of holiness he is with them, and the Shabbat delight that earns "a boundless inheritance ... and you shall spread out westward" is the holiness of Shabbat staying with a person into the weekdays. This is close to Rav Tzadok's reading of the third meal as holiness that goes with a person wherever he goes.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Tammuz 3:2: “So too the mitzvah of Shabbat, of which it is written, ‘On the day Hashem gives you rest from your sorrow and your trembling and from the labor,’ which is expounded in the holy Zohar (I 48b) of the day of Shabbat, that it is ‘the day of giving rest,’ when Hashem gives rest from the evil inclination and from all evil. Therefore it gives the reason, ‘And you shall remember that you were a slave ... and Hashem your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand ... therefore Hashem your God commanded you to keep the day of Shabbat,’ that is, that Israel can bring holiness into Shabbat. In these three mitzvos comes the remembrance of Egypt, for by remembering that Hashem brought us out then, though we were like a fetus in its mother’s womb, the light of the aspect of Atika shines in the heart, as it did at the Exodus.”
